title: Secrets, Supply Chain & Identity
summary: Lock down the last mile: Vault/Key Vault secret management with practiced rotation, the secrets-in-git ritual, SBOMs and cosign signing, least-privilege RBAC across five layers, and the Security+ domain crosswalk.
objectives: Manage secrets in Vault/Key Vault with dynamic credentials and rehearsed rotation
Prevent, detect, and remediate secrets committed to git with gitleaks gates
Generate SBOMs and sign container images, enforcing verification at deploy time
Apply least-privilege RBAC across Kubernetes, cloud, application, database, and pipeline layers
Map secrets and supply-chain work to CompTIA Security+ domains for panel conversations

notes.title: Secret Management: Vault and Key Vault
notes.body: Secrets — API keys, database passwords, TLS private keys — must live in a purpose-built secret store, never in code, config files, or chat. HashiCorp Vault and Azure Key Vault provide the same core contract: encrypted storage, fine-grained access policies, audit logging of every read, dynamic secrets (credentials generated on demand with a TTL, e.g. a database password that lives 1 hour), and rotation. The access pattern: the application authenticates to Vault (via Kubernetes auth, Azure auth, or AppRole — never a hardcoded token in production) and reads the secret at startup or via a sidecar injector; CI pipelines fetch secrets at runtime from the store instead of storing them as pipeline variables. Worked example: a Flask app needs the Postgres password. Anti-pattern: DATABASE_URL with the password in the deployment YAML committed to git. Solution: store it with vault kv put secret/checkout db_password=<value>; the pod uses the Vault agent injector annotation to render the secret into a file at startup; rotation is vault kv put with the new value plus a database password change — no redeploy, no git history. On Azure the equivalent is az keyvault secret set --vault-name kv-prod --name db-password, referenced from AKS via the Secrets Store CSI driver. The audit property is the point: the store logs who read what, when — something env vars and files can never do.

notes.title: Rotation and the Blast Radius of a Leak
notes.body: Every secret has a lifetime, and rotation is how you bound the blast radius when (not if) one leaks. Static secrets should rotate on a schedule (90 days is the common policy; 30 for high-value) and immediately on any suspected exposure, personnel departure, or the 'it was in a Slack thread' incident. Dynamic secrets are better: Vault generates a database credential per application instance with a 1-hour TTL — there is nothing long-lived to leak, and revocation is automatic. The rotation procedure must be rehearsed: (1) generate the new secret in the store; (2) update consumers (rolling restart or sidecar re-render); (3) verify the new credential works; (4) revoke the old one; (5) confirm nothing still uses it via the audit log. Worked example: an AWS access key was pasted into a public Slack channel. Solution sequence: immediately deactivate (not delete — preserve for forensics) the key in IAM, generate a replacement, update the one consumer via the secret store, verify, then delete the old key; search git history and logs for the key string; write the postmortem on how a long-lived key ended up copy-pasteable. The lesson the panel wants: the incident is survivable because rotation was a practiced procedure, not an improvisation — and the long-term fix is replacing the key with an OIDC-assumed role so there is no key to leak next time.

notes.title: Secrets in Git: The Antipattern and Its Detection
notes.body: Committing a secret to git publishes it to every clone, fork, and backup forever — deleting it later does not unpublish it, because history retains it. Prevention is a pipeline gate: gitleaks detect --no-git (or the pre-commit hook gitleaks protect) scans diffs for key patterns and fails the PR before the secret lands. Detection on existing repos: gitleaks detect --source . --verbose across history finds what is already burned. Remediation of a burned secret is a fixed ritual: (1) revoke/rotate the secret immediately — it is compromised, full stop; (2) purge it from history only if the repo can tolerate a force-push (git filter-repo), understanding clones still have it; (3) audit where the secret was valid during exposure (cloud audit logs); (4) add the gitleaks gate so it cannot recur. Worked example: gitleaks flags AKIA... in a commit from 6 months ago. Solution: the key is burned — rotate it now, check CloudTrail for usage of that key ID during the window, purge history if the team accepts the force-push, and enable the pre-commit hook today. The interview answer: 'A secret in git is a compromised secret; rotation first, history surgery second, prevention gate third.' Never 'we deleted the file so it is fine.'

notes.title: Supply Chain: SBOMs and Signing
notes.body: You cannot secure what you cannot inventory: an SBOM (Software Bill of Materials) lists every component in your artifact — OS packages, language dependencies, base image layers. Generate it in CI: syft packages myapp:tag -o spdx-json > sbom.json produces a machine-readable inventory you attach to the release. Signing proves the artifact you deploy is the artifact you built: cosign sign --key cosign.key myapp:tag (or keyless with OIDC via cosign sign --oidc-issuer) creates a signature; admission controllers verify it before pods start — unsigned images do not run. The chain: SBOM generation -> vulnerability scan of the SBOM -> sign the artifact -> verify at deploy time. Worked example: a critical CVE is announced in a base-image library at 9 AM. With SBOMs: query which of your 40 services' SBOMs contain the library version — 3 do; rebuild and resign those 3 by noon. Without SBOMs: manually audit 40 Dockerfiles and guess. Solution review: the SBOM turns a fire drill into a database query, and signing guarantees the rebuilt images are the ones that deploy. The panel framing: SBOM answers 'what is in it?', signing answers 'did we build it?', and together they are the supply-chain answer to 'how do you know what is running in prod?'

notes.title: RBAC and Least Privilege Across the Full Stack
notes.body: The panel asks about RBAC across a full-stack app — the answer spans every layer with one principle: least privilege, each identity getting only what its job requires. Kubernetes RBAC: Roles/ClusterRoles bound to ServiceAccounts via RoleBindings — the checkout ServiceAccount gets get/list on its own ConfigMaps, not cluster-admin. Cloud IAM: the patterns from M42/M43 (IRSA, Workload Identity) scoped to single buckets/queues. Application layer: role checks in the API (admin vs analyst vs viewer), row-level filtering on queries, and the database user granted SELECT on exactly the tables it needs. Pipeline: the deploy identity can apply to the staging namespace but needs an approval gate for prod. Worked example: design access for a data analyst who needs read-only dashboards. Solution: cloud IAM read-only role on the warehouse; Kubernetes read-only ClusterRole on the analytics namespace; application role 'viewer' with no export permission; database GRANT SELECT on the marts schema only; no CI deploy rights; no secret-store read. Every layer says the minimum. The failure mode is role explosion (400 custom roles nobody understands) — counter it with a small set of standard roles per layer, reviewed quarterly, with every exception carrying an owner and expiry, exactly like the M47 allowlist discipline.

notes.title: CompTIA Security+ Domain Crosswalk
notes.body: This module maps cleanly onto the CompTIA Security+ domains, which is useful interview framing: the domains are the industry's shared checklist, and narrating your work against them shows structured thinking. Domain 1 (General Security Concepts): least privilege, zero trust, and the control types your gates implement. Domain 2 (Threats, Vulnerabilities, and Mitigations): CVE triage, supply-chain attacks, and secret exposure as threat vectors. Domain 3 (Security Architecture): secret stores, signing infrastructure, and network segmentation for secret access. Domain 4 (Security Operations): rotation procedures, incident handling for leaks, log auditing of secret access, and vulnerability scanning operations. Domain 5 (Security Program Management): the allowlist governance, rotation policies, and compliance evidence (who accessed what secret when) that auditors ask for. Worked example: a panel asks 'how does your secrets program map to Security+?' Solution: 'Architecture gives us Vault/Key Vault with dynamic secrets; Operations gives us rotation runbooks and leak incident procedures with audit logs; Program Management gives us the 90-day rotation policy and the governed exception process — and the scanners from M47 feed the vulnerability management in Domain 4.' The point is not the certification — this course confers none — it is speaking the domain language that security-minded panels expect.

quiz.q: A Flask app needs the Postgres password. Which design is correct?
choices: DATABASE_URL with password in the committed deployment YAML
Vault KV secret rendered via agent injector; rotation without redeploy; audit log of reads
Password in a Slack pinned message
quiz.explain: The secret store gives encrypted storage, access policy, audit trail, and rotation without code changes. Committed YAML publishes the secret to every clone.

quiz.q: An AWS key is pasted into a public Slack channel. What is the FIRST step?
choices: Deactivate the key immediately (preserve for forensics), then replace via the secret store
Wait to see if it is misused
quiz.explain: The key is compromised the instant it is visible. Deactivate first (deleting destroys forensic evidence), replace, verify, then investigate usage.

quiz.q: Why are dynamic Vault database credentials better than a shared static password?
choices: Per-consumer credentials with a TTL: nothing long-lived to leak, revocation automatic
quiz.explain: Short-lived per-instance credentials bound the blast radius by construction; a leaked 1-hour credential dies on its own.

quiz.q: gitleaks flags AKIA... in a 6-month-old commit. Correct handling?
choices: Delete the file and move on
Rotate the key now (it is burned), audit usage during exposure, purge history only with team-accepted force-push, add the pre-commit gate
It is old so it is safe
quiz.explain: Age does not uncompromise a secret. Rotation first, exposure audit second, history surgery third (clones retain it anyway), prevention gate always.

quiz.q: A critical CVE is announced in a base-image library. With SBOMs in CI, what is your response?
choices: Query the SBOMs: which services contain the vulnerable version — rebuild, rescan, and resign exactly those
quiz.explain: The SBOM turns the fire drill into a database query: precise blast radius, targeted rebuilds, signed artifacts.

quiz.q: What does cosign verification at deploy time guarantee?
choices: The image is the artifact your pipeline built and signed — unsigned or tampered images never start
quiz.explain: Signing answers provenance ('did we build it?'), enforced by admission control. CVE scanning is the SBOM/scan job, a separate concern.

quiz.q: Design access for a read-only data analyst across the stack. Which is correct?
choices: Read-only warehouse role, read-only K8s ClusterRole on the analytics namespace, app viewer role, SELECT on marts schema only, no deploy or secret rights
quiz.explain: Least privilege at every layer, each scoped to the job. Any broader grant is a finding.

quiz.q: Your org has 400 custom IAM roles nobody understands. What is the fix?
choices: Consolidate to a small standard set per layer, quarterly review, exceptions with owner + expiry
quiz.explain: Role explosion is managed like the allowlist: standardize, review, and govern exceptions with ownership and expiry.

quiz.q: Map to Security+: quarterly rotation policy with audit evidence of secret access belongs to which domain?
quiz.explain: Policies, governance, and compliance evidence are Program Management; the rotation runbook itself is Operations (Domain 4).

handsOnLab.title: Lab: Vault, gitleaks gates, SBOMs, and signed images
handsOnLab.brief: You will run Vault in dev mode, wire secret injection into a sample app, plant and catch a git secret with gitleaks, generate SBOMs, sign an image with cosign, and verify the signature — the full supply-chain loop.
steps: Start Vault dev server: vault server -dev (dev only); export VAULT_ADDR and VAULT_TOKEN; enable KV v2 at secret/.
Store the app secret: vault kv put secret/labapp db_password='s3cret-lab-only'; create a policy allowing read on secret/labapp/*.
Deploy the sample app with the Vault agent injector annotation; exec into the pod and confirm the secret renders as a file with no secret in env or git.
Rotate: vault kv put a new value; restart the deployment; confirm the app picks it up with zero code changes.
Plant a fake AWS key in a commit; run gitleaks detect --source . --verbose; record the finding with commit SHA.
Execute the burned-secret ritual on paper: rotate (simulate), list what you would audit, and decide on history purge with justification.
Add the gitleaks pre-commit hook; attempt to commit another fake key and confirm the commit is blocked.
Build the app image; generate the SBOM: syft packages labapp:1.0 -o spdx-json > sbom.json; record the OS + language package counts.
Run trivy against the SBOM/image; for one finding, write the allowlist entry (ID, justification, owner, 14-day expiry).
Generate a cosign key pair; sign: cosign sign --key cosign.key labapp:1.0; verify: cosign verify --key cosign.pub labapp:1.0.

Simulate admission: write the policy snippet (e.g. Kyverno/Gatekeeper pseudo-policy) requiring valid cosign signatures on the lab namespace; confirm an unsigned tag would be rejected by your rule logic.
Write the Security+ crosswalk paragraph for your lab: which domain each piece belongs to. Tear down Vault and the images.
handsOnLab.deliverable: Working Vault-backed secret injection with a practiced rotation, a gitleaks-blocked commit, an SBOM, a signed and verified image, and an admission-policy sketch.
handsOnLab.checkpoint: Secret renders in-pod with nothing in git/env; gitleaks blocks the second fake key; cosign verify passes; the SBOM lists the vulnerable package you allowlisted.

mockTask.q: A developer committed a production database password 3 weeks ago and 'deleted the file' yesterday. What do you tell the team?
choices: The password is compromised: rotate it immediately, audit access during the 3-week window, purge history only if the team accepts a force-push, and add the gitleaks gate today
Only rotate if someone reports misuse
mockTask.explain: Deletion does not unpublish git history. The credential is burned until rotated; the exposure window must be audited; the gate prevents recurrence. 'Wait for misuse' is negligence.
